profiles.meeting_scenario: Two weeks after the successful 2-month pediatric pilot, an inpatient pediatric unit and the hospital-based home care agency are holding a coordination meeting to align the handoff workflow before expanding videoconference handoffs from one unit to both pediatric units for the next month's discharges. The meeting focuses on how the inpatient team will trigger the videoconference, what information must be ready at that point, how family participation will be arranged, and how equipment and first-visit planning will be handed off to home care. The expected outcome is a shared plan for when a case is marked ready, what gets sent to home care, and how each side will track completion without changing the overall pilot model.

members.name: Lauren Kim
members.expertise: Discharge coordination, inpatient care transitions, family teaching workflows on pediatric units
members.background: Lauren has worked for six years on a children's hospital medical-surgical floor and helped operationalize the pilot videoconference handoffs on one inpatient unit by fitting them into existing discharge planning rounds and bedside teaching routines.
members.private_state: She wants the expansion to feel lightweight for bedside staff and is trying to avoid adding extra documentation steps or delaying same-day discharges when plans are still moving.
hidden_assumptions: A handoff is functionally complete once the live videoconference has occurred and major concerns have been verbally reviewed, even if some chart documents finalize afterward.
Including family means having whichever parent or caregiver is physically present on the unit participate, since that is what staff can reliably coordinate during discharge preparation.
An equipment list shared before discharge can be preliminary and still useful, because home care can start planning from expected needs and reconcile details later.
When she says 'the discharge summary,' she means the inpatient physician's discharge documentation in the hospital EHR, which may not be signed at the exact time of the call.

members.name: Daniel Ortiz
members.role: Home Care Intake and Clinical Liaison, RN
members.expertise: Home care admissions, referral triage, start-of-care scheduling, durable medical equipment coordination
members.background: Daniel has spent eight years in pediatric home health, where he reviews hospital referrals, confirms home readiness, coordinates supplies with vendors, and ensures the admitting home care nurse has a usable packet before the first visit.
members.private_state: He wants the expanded process to produce dependable intake-ready information so his team can commit visit times and equipment delivery without last-minute callbacks after discharge.
hidden_assumptions: A handoff is not truly complete until home care has the documents and details needed to schedule the first visit and activate the referral in its intake queue.
Including family means the adult who will actually manage care at home should be on the call, even if that person is not the one currently at bedside.
An equipment list is actionable only when it reflects final ordered items, quantities, and delivery needs rather than expected or likely needs.
When he hears 'the discharge summary,' he assumes the referral packet or finalized transition document that home care can read immediately outside the inpatient workflow.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a completed handoff
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'mark the handoff complete' after the videoconference.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the handoff is complete once the call happens and key issues are verbally reviewed with home care and family, even if supporting documents or final orders appear later in the chart.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the handoff is complete only when the call is done and home care has enough finalized information to schedule start of care and move the referral out of pending intake.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds operationally routine, and both are trying to avoid delays, so neither pauses to define whether 'complete' refers to the conversation event or intake readiness.

misalignment_points.topic: Who it means to include family
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that 'family should be on the handoff call.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means whichever parent or guardian is present in the hospital room during discharge preparation should join the videoconference.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this means the adult who will provide hands-on care at home should participate, even if that requires separately connecting someone not physically at bedside.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both use the same patient-centered language and have no reason to suspect the other's boundary for 'family' differs, because each interpretation feels like the obvious intended inclusion.

misalignment_points.topic: Which discharge summary is being referenced
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the discharge summary' being available for the home care team.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the inpatient physician discharge note in the hospital EHR, which may be signed later the same day and is mainly part of the inpatient chart.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the referral-facing transition packet or finalized summary document that home care staff can immediately access and use for admission planning.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In hospital transitions, 'discharge summary' is a familiar umbrella term, so each assumes the other is referencing the same artifact without naming the file location or document type.

misalignment_points.topic: What the equipment list should contain
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the unit will 'send the equipment list by noon' for next-day discharges.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 plans to send an expected-needs list from morning rounds so home care can anticipate infusion supplies, enteral items, or pulse oximetry needs before final signatures are in place.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects a finalized list tied to signed orders, quantities, home address details, and delivery timing so vendors can actually be contacted and visits scheduled.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They agree on the deadline and the goal of avoiding delays, which masks that one sees the list as an early planning signal while the other sees it as an execution-ready document.

turns.inner_thought: The pilot worked because we tucked the video handoff into the discharge prep staff already do, instead of creating another separate checkpoint. If we're going to spread this to the second pediatric unit, I need the process to stay light: case manager, bedside nurse, and team pull it into rounds, do the live review, then keep moving. I do not want staff waiting around for every chart item to be finalized before they can say the handoff happened.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. The pilot on our unit went really well overall, and before both pediatric units start using the videoconference workflow next month, I want us to line up the discharge-day steps so everyone is working off the same playbook.

turns.inner_thought: Scaling is fine as long as 'ready' means intake-ready for us, not just that a conversation occurred. My team needs consistent triggers so we can move a referral from pending into active scheduling, assign a visit window, and get equipment moving without spending the afternoon chasing missing details. If they send the equipment list by noon, I need that to be something vendors can actually use, not a rough heads-up.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. From the home care side, we're ready to expand it as long as the trigger points are consistent enough that intake can plan first visits and equipment without a lot of extra back-and-forth.

turns.inner_thought: What I want documented operationally is simple: once the live videoconference has happened and we've talked through the major concerns, we should be able to mark the handoff complete. The bedside team can finish up teaching and the physician paperwork can catch up as it normally does. I don't want the unit held hostage by chart timing.
turns.utterance: Right, and my thought is that once the videoconference happens, we can mark the handoff complete and let the bedside team keep moving with the rest of discharge teaching.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly—if we're calling it a completed handoff, that should mean my staff can activate the referral, take it out of pending, and assign the first home visit window. Otherwise 'complete' doesn't help intake. Sounds like we're aligned on using the call as the point where the case becomes actionable.
turns.utterance: I agree with that. After a completed handoff, my team should be able to put the referral into the active admission queue and assign the first home visit window.

turns.inner_thought: Family should be on the handoff call, absolutely. In practice that usually means whichever parent or caregiver is in the room during late-morning discharge prep, because that's the person we can reliably pull into the video without adding a whole separate scheduling task. If we make this too complicated, staff won't stick with it.
turns.utterance: I also want family on the handoff call whenever we can make that happen. Usually the parent at bedside is available during that late-morning discharge prep window, so that's been workable.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, family should be on the handoff call—especially the adult who's actually going to manage feeds, line care, meds, or monitoring once the child is home. If that person hears the plan directly, we avoid a lot of confusion on the first visit. Good, it sounds like they're building family participation in.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. Having family on the handoff call really helps, especially when the person managing things at home hears the expectations directly around feeds, line care, or overnight monitoring.

turns.inner_thought: We can make sure the discharge summary is available before the call or shortly after because the team is already working that into the discharge workflow. In my mind that's the inpatient physician discharge documentation in the EHR; it may not be signed at the exact moment of the call, but it will be there as the day moves along. That should be enough without adding another document to chase.
turns.utterance: On the documentation side, the home care nurse should have the discharge summary before the call or shortly after, since the team is already building that into the discharge workflow.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the discharge summary is in the referral materials by the time the handoff closes out, my admitting nurse can review it right away and stop calling back for basics later in the afternoon. To me that's the usable transition packet on our side, not just something still living inside the inpatient chart. If that's what they're saying, great.
turns.utterance: That should work. As long as the discharge summary is in the referral materials when the handoff closes out, the admitting nurse can review it and avoid follow-up calls that afternoon.

turns.inner_thought: For next-day discharges, I can have the unit send the equipment list by noon based on morning rounds. It may still be an expected-needs list, but that's still useful for home care to start thinking through supplies, pulse ox, enteral items, whatever is likely. I don't want the unit waiting for every order signature just to give them a heads-up.
turns.utterance: And for next-day discharges, I think the unit can send the equipment list by noon so home care has a heads-up on likely supplies and devices.

turns.inner_thought: Noon is perfect if the equipment list is the final, actionable version with what is actually coming to the home. Then my team can start contacting vendors, align delivery timing, and build the start-of-care plan around it. Good—this gives us the lead time we need without waiting until discharge day.
turns.utterance: Noon works well from our side, because with the equipment list by then we can start lining up vendors and build the start-of-care plan around what is coming to the home.

turns.inner_thought: I need the second unit to mirror the first one closely: tie the video slot to discharge rounds, pull in whoever from family is present, do the verbal review, send the expected equipment list by noon for next-day cases, and keep staff burden low. If it feels like extra coordination layers, bedside nurses will push back and same-day discharges will bog down.
turns.utterance: Great. I'll ask the second pediatric unit to follow the same pattern and keep the videoconference slot tied to discharge rounds so the process stays simple for staff.

turns.inner_thought: This sounds like a solid workflow for expansion: intake will expect completed handoffs that are ready to move into active scheduling, family participation from the person handling care at home, the discharge summary in the referral packet, and the equipment list in time to execute vendor planning. If my nurses hear it this way, we should be able to absorb the second unit smoothly.
turns.utterance: This sounds like a solid shared workflow. I'll let the intake nurses know to expect completed handoffs, family participation, the discharge summary, and the equipment list in that sequence.
